source.title: Unforgettable Generalization in Language Models
source.authors: Eric Zhang; Leshem Choshen; Jacob Andreas

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendix; no apparent cutoff affecting the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: Tests random-label fine-tuning in language models and measures held-out task behavior, a related method and setting for the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly says the models learn near-random predictions on individual training examples used for forgetting, but does not report training accuracy on those randomized labels. Figure-only task and model values are not transcribed. Cited prior-work findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses random-label fine-tuning to investigate skill forgetting. Appendix A specifies that labels are resampled each epoch, rather than fixed as a random labeling to memorize. Results measure accuracy against true labels and generalization of forgetting, without reporting error against fixed randomized training targets. They therefore do not test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: random-response fine-tuning produces task-dependent generalization of forgetting, largely governed by the evaluation task, and even successful output-level forgetting is shallow because linear probes can recover task information.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tuning language models on randomized responses to forget capabilities; evaluates held-out language-task behavior rather than image classification training error and test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies across evaluation tasks; commonsense reasoning tasks are described as more resilient than lower-level linguistic acceptability and entailment tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: After random-response fine-tuning, held-out task performance varies substantially: commonsense tasks often retain above-chance accuracy, while some linguistic tasks approach chance. Cross-task forgetting depends strongly on the evaluation task, with broadly similar trends across the three models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization of skill forgetting through random-response fine-tuning depends on the evaluated capability.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6 reports modest anticorrelation between example learning and forgetting orders, using confidence thresholds and excluding examples never learned or forgotten.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Examples learned earlier during task fine-tuning tend to be forgotten later during subsequent random-response fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes retain task performance after random-response fine-tuning, including when output accuracy approaches chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-response fine-tuning can suppress task outputs while preserving task information accessible through linear probes.

record.problems: Random-label training accuracy is not reported. Most task-specific results are displayed in figures without tabulated values. The supplied text describes held-out accuracy but does not report uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Task-specific Figure 2 values, cross-task Figure 3 values, reduced-dataset Figure 7 values, and flipped-label Figure 8 values are figure/table-layout results not transcribed as individual rows; they exceed the useful row coverage available here. No result for a claim version other than V1 is reported.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero error on a fixed completely randomized training labeling, chance test performance after such fitting, and fitting without changing training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across increasing fractions of fixed random-label corruption.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels. Sequential correct-label training and random-response forgetting do not measure this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: Near-random predictions on training examples do not demonstrate memorization of assigned random labels, especially when targets are resampled each epoch. Remove the extracted V1 limits_scope verdict. No omitted result establishes a test of another claim version.

versions.untested_parts: Image classification; explicit training error on randomized labels; comparison showing the same networks generalize well on true labels.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7B
rows.stage_stated: base model, then fine-tuned on each task before random-label forgetting
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on randomized labels from each task’s training set, then evaluated on the held-out task test set.

conditions.value: 21 multiple-choice tasks; up to 1000 examples per set
random labels; 100 epochs or until test accuracy drops below 50%

rows.measure: Held-out task accuracy after random-label fine-tuning, compared with 50% chance accuracy.
rows.value: The authors state that many tasks do not return to the expected accuracy of 50% after forgetting.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result across tasks; the paper also reports that outcomes vary widely, with commonsense reasoning more resilient and lower-level linguistic acceptability and entailment classification more forgettable. No randomized-label training accuracy is reported.
rows.check: Held-out true-label accuracy measures retained task capability, not successful fitting of randomized training labels. Above-chance accuracy cannot establish partial fitting or challenge V1. Appendix A also specifies fresh random response selection each epoch and different learning rates for correct-label fine-tuning (0.003) and forgetting (0.0001). The 99% training-accuracy stopping criterion applies to correct-label fine-tuning.

rows.subject: GPT-J-6B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on random labels for cross-task forgetting; evaluated on task test sets.
rows.measure: Cross-task forget ratio, shown in Figure 9.
rows.note: The text says the forget-ratio trends are broadly the same as for LLaMA-2-7B, but the plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Cross-task forget ratios measure loss of true-label task performance, not error on randomized training targets. Figure 9 contains numerical annotations in the supplied text, so 'figure only' overstates the lack of values; however, one aggregate row cannot represent the task-pair results.

reader_labels.condition: LLaMA-2-7B across the tested language tasks
reader_labels.reason: Held-out accuracy often remains above chance after random-label fine-tuning, and the degree of forgetting varies by task (R1). The study does not establish zero randomized-label training error.
